title: Mauna Loa Lava and Light Pillar Caught on Camera from Gemini North
caption: Mauna Loa's lava glow and a lava light pillar, seen from Maunakea, Hawaiʻi

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The reddish glow of Mauna Loa's lava flows appears in this night view, recorded by a Cloudcam belonging to the International Gemini Observatory. The camera sits close to Maunakea's snowy summit, which is the highest point in the frame. The camera runs around the clock. Also visible is an exceptionally rare lava light pillar.

Mauna Loa, a volcano on the island of Hawaiʻi, started erupting on 27 November 2022, as lava broke out of fissures in Moku‘āweoweo, the caldera at its summit. Described as the world's largest active volcano, it had not erupted in nearly 40 years, and the glow of its flows could be seen across the island. This picture was taken at 02:15 local time on 29 November.

Light pillars are more often seen with the Sun. A lava pillar needs a rare combination: an erupting volcano to provide light near the horizon, plus high-altitude cloud and freezing temperatures. Together these produce millions of ice crystals floating horizontally, which reflect the light toward the observer.

understand.summary: A photograph from one of Gemini's Cloudcams, a camera that runs continuously near the Maunakea summit; no filters or exposure details are published.
understand.eye: The caption gives no exposure details, so it is unclear how closely the brightness of the glow and pillar matches what an eye would see.

explore: Staff at Gemini North and the other Maunakea Observatories watched closely as flows moved down Mauna Loa's flank toward the Daniel K. Inouye Highway (Saddle Road). On Mauna Loa itself, lava crossed the access road to NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory and cut its power, though the eruption posed no threat to the Maunakea observatories.
alt: A night view from Maunakea's snow-covered summit showing the reddish glow of lava flows and a lava light pillar.
